articles.title: The Attention Economy and Deep Work
articles.content:
Digital platforms compete for a scarce resource: human attention. Notifications, infinite feeds, and autoplay are engineered to keep users engaged for as long as possible. Economists describe this as an attention economy, in which the product is not the content itself but the audience sold to advertisers.

Knowledge workers pay a hidden tax. Even brief interruptions can force a restart of complex thinking, and studies of task-switching show measurable losses in accuracy and speed. Some professionals respond by scheduling 'deep work' blocks—periods free of email and chat—while others negotiate team norms that treat instant replies as optional rather than expected.

Critics argue that individual discipline cannot offset system design. If platforms profit from distraction, they will optimise for it. Policy responses range from transparency requirements to limits on dark patterns that trick users into longer sessions. The deeper question is cultural: whether a society treats sustained attention as a private virtue or as infrastructure worth protecting.

questions.question: What is the real product in the attention economy?
questions.explanation: 原文：the product is not the content itself but the audience sold to advertisers.

questions.question: What is a 'deep work' block?
options: A period of uninterrupted focused work
questions.explanation: 原文：periods free of email and chat.

questions.question: Why do critics doubt individual discipline alone?
options: Because platforms optimise for distraction when it is profitable
questions.explanation: 原文：If platforms profit from distraction, they will optimise for it.

questions.question: What does the author treat as the deeper issue?
options: Whether attention is protected as infrastructure
questions.explanation: 末段：whether a society treats sustained attention as a private virtue or as infrastructure worth protecting.

articles.title: Urban Mobility After the Car Peak
articles.content:
In several wealthy cities, car ownership among young adults has declined even as incomes recovered. Analysts debate whether this is a temporary reaction to housing costs or a structural shift toward shared and active transport. Ride-hailing, e-bikes, and improved transit corridors all compete with private cars for short and medium trips.

Parking policy quietly shapes outcomes. Where street parking is cheap and abundant, driving remains attractive. Where cities price curb space and convert lanes to bus or cycle routes, mode share moves faster. Employers also matter: transit benefits and secure bike storage influence commuting more than slogans about sustainability.

None of this eliminates cars. Freight, night shifts, and suburban distances still rely on them. The realistic goal is a portfolio: dense cores with strong transit, suburbs with safe cycling links, and pricing that reflects congestion and land use. Cities that treat mobility as a system—rather than a race between vehicles—tend to move more people with less friction.

questions.question: What trend is observed in some wealthy cities?
options: Young adults own fewer cars despite income recovery
questions.explanation: 原文：car ownership among young adults has declined even as incomes recovered.

questions.question: Which policy most directly shifts mode share?
options: Pricing curb space and converting lanes to bus or cycle routes
questions.explanation: 原文：Where cities price curb space and convert lanes... mode share moves faster.

questions.question: Why will cars not disappear entirely?
options: Because freight, night shifts and suburbs still need them
questions.explanation: 原文：Freight, night shifts, and suburban distances still rely on them.

questions.question: What does the author recommend?
options: A single vehicle type for all trips
A mobility portfolio treated as a system
questions.explanation: 末段：treat mobility as a system... a portfolio of solutions.

articles.title: Scientific Peer Review Under Pressure
articles.content:
Peer review remains the main gatekeeper of scholarly quality, yet it is under strain. Submission volumes have grown, reviewers are unpaid, and turnaround expectations have shortened. Journals experiment with open review, reviewer recognition, and AI tools that flag methodological weaknesses before human reading.

Open peer review—where identities or reports are public—aims to improve accountability. Evidence on quality is mixed: some studies find more civil tone and clearer critiques, others note that junior scholars may fear retaliation. Registered reports, in which journals accept a study based on its question and method before results exist, reduce publication bias toward surprising findings.

Technology can assist but not replace judgement. Automated checks catch missing data files and statistical red flags, yet cannot judge whether a research question matters. The enduring task is social: sustaining a community willing to scrutinise work carefully without turning review into a barrier that protects incumbents.

questions.question: What pressure does peer review face?
options: Growing submissions and unpaid, time-pressed reviewers
questions.explanation: 原文：Submission volumes have grown, reviewers are unpaid, and turnaround expectations have shortened.

questions.question: What is a potential downside of open review?
questions.explanation: 原文：junior scholars may fear retaliation.

questions.question: How do registered reports help?
options: They accept papers only after results
They reduce bias toward surprising results
questions.explanation: 原文：reduce publication bias toward surprising findings.

questions.question: What can technology NOT do in review?
options: Judge whether a research question matters
questions.explanation: 原文：cannot judge whether a research question matters.
